_comment: What the scheduler DOES with per-hart-width profiles. DroNet and the 64x96 detector, both profiled on 1/2/4/8 harts (topo_0, topo_0_1, topo_0_1_2_3, topo_0_1_2_3_4_5_6_7), solved in shard mode so the solver picks a WIDTH PER DISPATCH rather than being told one for the model. This is the consumption side of the multi-core profiles committed in 58e042d / faa78cb / b45bc93.
_why_this_spec_exists: The per-dispatch measurement (out/figures/k1_multicore_scaling.png) shows that sharding gain varies 4.8x WITHIN one model -- 4.02x on a wide-OC conv down to 0.83x on a 1x1. That says no single core width is right for a model. It does not by itself show that a solver can exploit it. This spec is the other half: the same profiles, handed to the scheduler, with the widths it chose recorded in the schedule.
_capabilities_comment: IME is measured, not assumed: smt.vmadot executes on cores 0-3 and SIGILLs on 4-7 (artifacts/k1_bringup/*/ime_capability_probe.txt). Not exercised here -- these are rvv_x60 profiles and the question is core WIDTH, not implementation.
_topo_comment: topo_tag_override is FALSE, and that is the whole point. With it true every combination is costed from topo_0, so a 4-hart block would be charged the SINGLE-hart time while occupying four harts -- the solver would correctly never choose one, and the run would report 'sharding does not help' for a purely clerical reason. Each block is costed from its own N-hart profile, which the combination's topo tag selects.
_instances_comment: Pinned, not derived. The horizon heuristic sizes instance counts from the profiles, so a faster configuration produces FEWER releases and two solves stop being comparable -- see schedule_scoring.instances_per_model and the guard in compare_candidates.
